correctness.rationale: The map x=−cot(πu) has Jacobian π csc²(πu); multiplication by the tilted Gaussian density yields exactly g_a and integral (2γ)^(−1/2). Near zero, cot²(πu)=(πu)^(−2)−2/3+O(u²), so g_a∼(√(π/2)e^(2γ/3)/π²)u^(−2)exp(−γ/(π²u²)), with the same behavior at one by reflection. On complex disks of radius κu about small positive u the real part of cot² is bounded below by b/u², and the csc² factor by C/u² in modulus. Cauchy's estimates give C r! κ^(−r) u^(−r−2) exp(−bγ/u²); for fixed r the bound tends to zero, justifying all flat endpoint derivatives, and maximization over u gives A B^r(r!)^(3/2) using Stirling. Uniform analytic disks handle the compact interior. Flatness and Taylor remainders for a putative order 1<s<3/2 give |g_a(u)|≤A(Bu)^r(r!)^(s−1) for every r, and optimizing forces exp(−b u^(−1/(s−1))), incompatible with the positive asymptotic. Monotonicity in s excludes orders ≤1 as well. Absolute Fourier convergence allows the n-point sum to retain only frequencies ℓn; Parseval in the one uniform U proves the exact variance and zero-frequency unbiasedness. Integration by parts with r proportional to |k|^(2/3) gives stretched-exponential coefficients; in the variance sum one can split the exponent using n^(2/3)|ℓ|^(2/3)≥(n^(2/3)+|ℓ|^(2/3))/2. Conversely RMS dominates |ĝ(n)| at each n. If a faster envelope held, reality would give it on both signs of k; splitting the exponent in half and maximizing x^r exp(−c x^β/2) proves a derivative bound of order 1/β (or use any smaller β still above 2/3). Finitely many possible exceptions could be absorbed by increasing the prefactor, so failure is infinite, not necessarily at every n. The finite floating-point verifier was inspected, not run, and cannot prove the rates.
residual_risks: Exact arithmetic, fixed parameter a, one shared shift and RMS only. No matching every-n lower bound, absolute exponent constant, machine-stability claim, or uniformity approaching a=1/2.

evidence: The Möbius rule supplies fixed-order algebraic Sobolev bounds and an algebraic randomized theorem with randomized count as well as shift. Ouyang–Wang–He use Student-t proposals and scrambled-net settings in their algebraic RMSE estimates. Trefethen–Weideman already obtain an exponent 2/3 in a Gaussian-decay example by balancing mesh and truncation errors on a real-line trapezoid.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Neither general fixed-order estimates nor an earlier exponent for another integrand and numerical rule give the fixed-n sharp uniform RMS envelope. Standard Gevrey–Fourier theory supplies the order-to-envelope implications, conditional on knowing the exact class.

evidence: Algebraic bounds for every finite Sobolev order do not prescribe the growth of constants in the order, much less exclude all faster exponents. A Gaussian tail with a truncated real-line mesh gives no coefficient lower-envelope obstruction for cotangent-periodized data. Here the obstruction uses the precise nonzero flat asymptotic and the presence of ĝ(n) at count n.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The fixed-target exact classification needs a quantitative upper and lower regularity analysis, not just substitution into the prior quadrature theorems. Aliasing then transfers the obstruction to this specific fixed-count randomization.

originality.rationale: The cotangent mapping and shifted trapezoid framework are established; applying the same map to the tilted Gaussian is exactly a Möbius trapezoid. The inspected sources do not establish or mechanically imply this integrand's exact Gevrey order and the sharp fixed-count RMS envelope. Value and novelty attach to that exact rate characterization, not the mapping, alias identity, or use of Gevrey theory itself.
residual_risks: Specialized Fourier saddle asymptotics or rational spectral approximation results not surfaced could imply the same exponent. Priority is limited to inspected passages and to this exact claim, not its classical underlying tools.

value.rationale: The result tells a user of the existing Möbius rule exactly what speed can be guaranteed, uniformly over sample sizes, for a natural unbounded Gaussian moment. It separates strict stretched-exponential behavior from both the weaker superalgebraic statement and an unattainable exponential envelope. Using exact flatness to rule out faster convergence avoids inferring a lower bound from finite samples or assuming that oscillatory Fourier terms have uniform pointwise size.
residual_risks: The result neither compares optimal quadrature methods for a known Gaussian integral nor gives a finite-precision error guarantee.
